name: Nepal: the Khumbu, Annapurna, Langtang and the valley

destination.name: Nepal: the Khumbu, Annapurna, Langtang and the valley
destination.pitch: The trek is the trip and the towns are only beds: twelve days minimum, October to November or March to April, and everything else here is what you do while you acclimatise or wait out a flight.

because.nature: Eight of the fourteen 8,000m peaks are in this country, and the Annapurna Sanctuary at 4,130m is the only place in the Himalaya where you stand inside a closed ring of 7,000m walls.
because.exploration: Whole valleys still have no road: Langtang is a nine-hour jeep and a four-day walk from a capital 60km away, and the Khumbu is reached by a 527m sloping runway or six days on foot.
because.food: Dal bhat with unlimited refills is the best value hot meal anywhere, and Newari cooking in the valley is genuinely distinct. Above Namche you eat what a porter carried up, and it shows.
because.relaxation: Almost none. Lodge rooms are unheated plywood, the stove is lit at 17:00, and the only real rest is Pokhara's lakeside or a hot spring at Jhinu on the way out.
because.culture: Seven UNESCO monument zones in one valley, Newar woodcarving that survived 1934 and 2015, working cremation ghats at Pashupatinath, and Sherpa gompas at 3,900m that are not museums.
because.adventure: Kala Patthar at 5,545m, Thorong La at 5,416m, Tserko Ri at 4,984m, and a flight into Lukla that is cancelled for days at a time. Altitude here is a medical risk, not a metaphor.
because.city: Kathmandu is loud, dusty and worth two nights for the squares, the permits and the gear shops. The winter air is genuinely bad. It is not why you came.

destination.caveat: Monsoon from June to September closes most of this: leeches, landslides, no views, cancelled flights. That leaves October to November and March to April. Since April 2023 a guide is formally required in the parks, the acclimatisation days are not optional, and Lukla strands people for days. Put toge Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

cities.name: Kathmandu
cities.base: Thamel for gear shops, permit agents and the airport taxi rank within five minutes. Patan, across the Bagmati, if you would rather sleep somewhere quiet and beautiful and taxi in. Lazimpat splits it.

cities.name: Bhaktapur
cities.base: Nobody has to sleep here, but those who do get the squares at 06:00 empty. Thirteen kilometres east of Kathmandu, 45 to 90 minutes depending on the Ring Road. A half day, or a morning and a night.

cities.name: Nagarkot
cities.base: A ridge at 2,175m with two dozen hotels all facing one way. Sleep here only for the sunrise, and only October to December when the haze lifts. Otherwise it is a 90 minute drive to look at cloud.

cities.name: Bandipur
cities.base: The one pedestrian street at the top of the hill, 8km up a switchback road off the Prithvi Highway. Book on the bazaar itself, not down in Dumre. One night, on the drive between Kathmandu and Pokhara.

cities.name: Pokhara
cities.base: Lakeside, north end, towards the Hallan Chowk and Baidam blocks. The south end near Damside is cheaper and dead at night. Old Bazaar, 4km northeast, is the real town and has almost no beds.

cities.name: Sarangkot
cities.base: A ridge at 1,592m above Pokhara with a handful of lodges and the paragliding launch. Forty five minutes by taxi, or a two hour walk up from Lakeside. Go up in the dark, come down under a wing.

cities.name: Ghandruk
cities.base: A Gurung village at 1,940m of slate roofs and stone stairs, Annapurna South filling the sky behind it. Jeep from Pokhara in three hours to the car park, then 20 minutes of steps with your bag.

cities.name: Ghorepani
cities.base: A lodge village on a 2,874m saddle, reached only on foot: five to six hours up from Hile via the Ulleri staircase. Book on the Poon Hill side of the pass so the 04:30 start is 45 minutes.

cities.name: Sauraha, Chitwan
cities.base: Sauraha, on the Rapti opposite the park boundary. The lodges inside the buffer forest at Bachhauli are quieter and you hear more at night. Six hours by road from Kathmandu, five from Pokhara.

cities.name: Lukla
cities.base: Two thousand eight hundred and forty five metres, one street, the airstrip at the end of it. You sleep here the night you fly in or before you fly out, never by choice. Book near the gate.

cities.name: Namche Bazaar
cities.base: The horseshoe of lodges at 3,440m above the Dudh Koshi. Sleep high in the bowl near the gompa, not by the arch: the walk up is the acclimatisation. Six to seven hours on foot from Lukla.

cities.name: Dingboche
cities.base: Four thousand four hundred and ten metres, stone-walled potato fields, no trees. The upper row of lodges gets an extra hour of sun and the Ama Dablam view. Two nights, not one.

cities.name: Gorak Shep
cities.base: Five thousand one hundred and sixty four metres on the sand of a drained lake, four lodges, no plumbing worth the name. One night, and you will not sleep well. Nobody should spend two.

cities.name: Syabrubesi
cities.base: Fourteen hundred and sixty metres at the Langtang roadhead, lodges either side of a suspension bridge. One night, because the jeep from Kathmandu takes seven to nine hours and arrives spent.

cities.name: Kyanjin Gompa
cities.base: Three thousand eight hundred and seventy metres at the head of the Langtang valley: a dozen lodges, a cheese factory, a glacier. Two nights, because Tserko Ri needs the second morning.

cities.name: Annapurna Base Camp and the Sanctuary
cities.base: There are lodges at Machhapuchhre and Annapurna Base Camp, but they are trek stages: you arrive, sleep once at 4,130m, and walk back out the way you came in. Chhomrong is the real base.

cities.name: Mardi Himal High Camp
cities.base: High Camp at 3,580m: six lodges on a bare ridge, Machhapuchhre 3km away, no water source. You reach it on day three out of Pokhara, and the trek turns on whether it has beds free.

cities.name: Poon Hill
cities.base: Three thousand two hundred and ten metres, a steel tower, a tea stall and two hundred people at 06:15 in November. Nothing up here but the view, walked up from Ghorepani in the dark.

cities.name: Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar
cities.base: No beds at either. Base camp is a moraine with expedition tents on it April to May and nothing in October. Both are walked from Gorak Shep, the only place you can sleep to reach them.

outings.name: Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar

startsFrom.name: Kathmandu, for the Lukla or Manthali flight

outings.why: Twelve to fourteen days on foot from Lukla, five to seven hours most days, two of them rest days at Namche and Dingboche that are not optional. Kala Patthar at 5,545m is the view; base camp at 5,364m is the errand.
outings.season: Mid Oct to Nov and late Mar to mid May. Shut in monsoon.
outings.fallback: Turn at Dingboche or Lobuche and walk out; the trek is not worth pulmonary or cerebral oedema, and the helicopter off the glacier costs five figures.

outings.name: The Gokyo Lakes and Gokyo Ri
outings.why: Nine to eleven days up the Dudh Koshi instead of the Khumbu, to six turquoise lakes at 4,700m and a 5,357m hill with a better Everest view than Kala Patthar. Half the traffic, and the Cho La at 5,420m links it to base camp.
outings.season: Mid Oct to Nov, Apr to mid May. Cho La needs no fresh snow.
outings.fallback: Gokyo Ri and the fourth and fifth lakes, then back down the way you came, skipping the Cho La entirely.

outings.name: Kala Patthar at dawn
outings.why: Three hundred and eighty metres from Gorak Shep, leaving at 04:30, two to three hours up at 5,200m plus. Minus 20C in the wind is normal and there is nowhere to shelter. The whole trek is arranged around this one morning.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Mar to May. Clear before 08:00 or not at all.
outings.fallback: Base camp and back, four hours, 200m of moraine and no altitude gain beyond 5,364m.

outings.name: Namche to Tengboche and back
outings.why: Two hours contouring with Ama Dablam ahead, 600m down to the river at Phunki Tenga, then 600m straight up through juniper to the monastery at 3,867m. Sit at the back of the 15:00 puja. Everyone underestimates the climb out.
outings.season: All year on foot; Oct to Nov and Mar to May for the views.
outings.fallback: Khumjung and the Everest View Hotel, five hours, same acclimatisation and half the descent.

outings.name: The Everest View acclimatisation day
outings.why: Four hundred and forty metres up to Syangboche and the Hotel Everest View terrace at 3,880m, on to Khumjung, then back down to sleep at 3,440m. Climb high, sleep low, and the day that decides whether you get past Dingboche.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Mar to May. Snow can close the Syangboche path.
outings.fallback: The park visitor centre and the Sherpa Culture Museum, three hours, still 100m of climbing.

outings.name: The Lukla flight
outings.why: Thirty five minutes into a 527m sloping runway at 2,845m, flown visually, and cancelled for days at a time in cloud. In peak season it departs from Manthali instead, four to five hours' drive east, leaving Kathmandu at about 01:00.
outings.season: All year, least reliable Jun to Sep. Mornings only.
outings.fallback: A helicopter seat share for 500 dollars and up, or the six-day walk in from Jiri, which is how it was done before 1964.

outings.name: The Annapurna Sanctuary to Annapurna Base Camp
outings.why: Seven to eleven days from Nayapul or Ghandruk up a closing gorge to a 4,130m amphitheatre ringed by 7,000m walls. The Hinku Cave section avalanches and has killed people; cross it early and not after fresh snow.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Mar to Apr. Avalanche risk Dec to Feb.
outings.fallback: Ghandruk to Chhomrong and back over four days, which gets the villages and the Annapurna South face without entering the gorge.

outings.name: The Poon Hill and Ghorepani to Ghandruk loop
outings.why: Four to five days: the Ulleri staircase, a night at 2,874m, Poon Hill at dawn, then the ridge to Tadapani and down through Ghandruk. The shortest trek in Nepal that still crosses 3,000m and the right one on a twelve-day trip.
outings.season: Oct to Dec and Mar to Apr for rhododendron.
outings.fallback: Australian Camp and Dhampus from Kande, two days, 2,000m at the top and one night in a lodge.

outings.name: Poon Hill at sunrise
outings.why: Forty five minutes and 340m up in the dark from Ghorepani to a steel tower at 3,210m facing Dhaulagiri. In late October there are two hundred people on it by 06:15; stay twenty minutes after they leave and it empties.
outings.season: Oct to Dec clearest. Cloud from Mar, useless Jun to Sep.
outings.fallback: Stay in the dining room, because in cloud there is nothing up there and the path down is slippery in the dark.

outings.name: Mardi Himal High Camp and the Viewpoint
outings.why: Four to five days on a ridge nobody walked before 2012: two days in cloud forest, then High Camp at 3,580m with Machhapuchhre 3km away, and the exposed scree to 4,200m. Six lodges up top and no water source.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Mar to Apr. Ridge is dangerous in snow.
outings.fallback: Turn at High Camp and skip the upper viewpoint; the Machhapuchhre view is the same and the scree is what hurts people.

outings.name: The Langtang valley to Kyanjin Gompa
outings.why: Seven to eight days and the closest real trek to Kathmandu, up a sheer river gorge to 3,870m under Langtang Lirung. The 2015 earthquake killed around 250 people in Langtang village; the valley rebuilt and the trekkers have not come back.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Mar to May. Rhododendron in April.
outings.fallback: Syabrubesi to Lama Hotel and back, three days, the gorge and the langur monkeys without the altitude.

outings.name: Tserko Ri
outings.why: Eleven hundred metres from Kyanjin, four hours up and two down, leaving at 04:30 to beat the cloud. Nearly five thousand metres, a full circle of Langtang Lirung, Langshisa Ri and the Tibetan frontier. The best day in the valley.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Apr to May. Snow on top into early spring.
outings.fallback: Kyanjin Ri, three hours and 430m, prayer flags and most of the same view.

outings.name: The jeep to Syabrubesi
outings.why: Seven to nine hours for 120km: tarmac to Trishuli, then single-lane gravel cut into a gorge wall with a 500m drop and annual landslide repairs. Leave by 07:00 or you finish in the dark, and take the front seats.
outings.season: All year; landslide closures common Jul to Sep.
outings.fallback: A shared helicopter to Syabrubesi in 45 minutes, about 400 dollars a seat when there are four of you.

outings.name: Kathmandu valley on foot
outings.why: Swayambhunath at 06:30 before the coaches, the Durbar Square and Asan Tole before 10:00, Patan and its museum after lunch, Boudhanath at dusk for the kora. Four of the valley's seven UNESCO zones in one day, and taxis between them.
outings.season: All year. Oct to Nov clearest, worst air Jan to Mar.
outings.fallback: The Patan Museum and Krishna Mandir, then the Garden of Dreams, all indoors or shaded.

outings.name: Bhaktapur and Changu Narayan
outings.why: Forty five to ninety minutes east to a walled Newar town where the NPR 1,800 ticket lasts several days, then 20 minutes on to a temple with a 464 AD inscription in the courtyard. Sleep in Bhaktapur and you get the squares empty at 06:00.
outings.season: All year. Pottery Square does not work in monsoon.
outings.fallback: Bhaktapur alone, four hours, with juju dhau and the Peacock Window lane.

outings.name: Chitwan: the canoe, the jungle walk and the jeep
outings.why: Dugout canoe on the Rapti at 06:30 among the crocodiles, then four hours on foot in the core area with two unarmed guides, about 700 rhino and roughly 125 tigers. Rhino are the actual danger and people are hurt most years.
outings.season: Oct to Mar. Grass is cut Jan, sightings best then.
outings.fallback: The canoe plus the elephant breeding centre and a Tharu village walk, half a day, no core-area permit needed.

outings.name: Sarangkot sunrise and the paraglide down
outings.why: Taxi up at 05:00 to 1,592m for Dhaulagiri, the Annapurnas and Machhapuchhre going pink over a lake full of cloud, then launch tandem at about 09:00 and land on the shore 1,000m below.
outings.season: Oct to Dec clearest. No flying in monsoon.
outings.fallback: Sunrise only, then walk the ridge west to Naudanda for four flat hours with the range beside you.

outings.name: Phewa Lake and the World Peace Pagoda
outings.why: Row out at 06:30 while the water is flat enough to hold the reflection, land on the far shore and climb 45 minutes through forest to the stupa at 1,113m, then walk the ridge on to Pumdikot. The taxi to the door removes the point.
outings.season: All year. Reflections only before about 08:00.
outings.fallback: The International Mountain Museum and the Old Bazaar, both fine in rain.

outings.name: Bandipur: Thani Mai, the Tundikhel and Ramkot
outings.why: Thirty minutes of steps at dawn to a temple facing the Annapurna to Manaslu wall, then three flat hours out along the ridge to a Magar village of round thatched houses where nothing is for sale. The best short walk in central Nepal.
outings.season: All year. Oct to Feb for the mountain view.
outings.fallback: Siddha Gufa, three and a half hours, a 50m cave chamber and a steep slippery descent to reach it.

outings.name: Thorong La and the Annapurna Circuit
outings.why: Twelve to sixteen days round the massif over a 5,416m pass, from paddy to Tibetan desert in one trek. Jeep roads now reach Manang and Muktinath, so most people walk the Manang to Jomsom half and take a vehicle to the ends.
outings.season: Oct to Nov, Apr to May. Pass shuts with snow in winter.
outings.fallback: Jomsom to Muktinath and the Kali Gandaki gorge in three days, flying in from Pokhara and out again.

places.name: Kathmandu Durbar Square
places.note: Still visibly the 2015 earthquake's worst urban day: Kasthamandap only reopened in 2022 and Maju Deval was rebuilt from photographs. The ticket also gets you the Kumari Ghar courtyard, where the living goddess appears at a window most afternoons.

places.name: Swayambhunath
places.note: Three hundred and sixty five steep steps up the east face to a 5th-century stupa and the whole valley laid out in the haze. Go at 06:30 with the Newar circumambulators; by 10:00 it is coaches, and the macaques will take food out of your hand.

places.name: Boudhanath stupa
places.note: Thirty six metres of whitewashed dome in a ring of Tibetan monasteries; the spire came down in 2015 and was rebuilt within eighteen months, largely on donations. Walk the kora clockwise at dusk when the butter lamps go on and the crowd is Tibetan rather than foreign.

places.name: Pashupatinath
places.note: Nepal's main Shiva temple and its working cremation ghats. Non-Hindus cannot enter the inner temple and should watch from the east bank terraces, at a distance, without a camera pointed at a family. Aarti at the Bachhareshwari ghat around 18:00.

places.name: Patan Durbar Square and Krishna Mandir
places.note: The best of the three Durbar Squares and the least wrecked: Krishna Mandir, a 1637 stone shikhara of 21 gilded finials, came through both 1934 and 2015 standing. Late afternoon light hits the palace facade and the square empties out by six.

places.name: Patan Museum
places.note: The one museum in Nepal that is properly curated: about 200 bronzes and gilt-copper repousse pieces in a restored palace wing, with labels written by someone who understood the iconography. An hour and a half, and the courtyard cafe behind it is quiet.

places.name: Garden of Dreams
places.note: A 1920s Rana neoclassical garden restored by the Austrians in 2007, and the only place within walking distance of Thamel where the traffic noise drops. Worth the entry on your first afternoon when the jet lag hits and you cannot face a temple.

places.name: Asan Tole and the Indra Chowk lanes
places.note: Six lanes meeting at a spice and vegetable crossroads that has been the city's wholesale market for centuries; the walk south to Indra Chowk goes through the bead sellers and the blanket shops. Go before 09:00, and accept that you will be pushed along.

places.name: Narayanhiti Palace Museum
places.note: The royal palace, opened as a museum after the monarchy ended in 2008. The point of going is the Tribhuvan Sadan wing, demolished to its footings, where Prince Dipendra shot nine of his family in 2001; the bullet holes are marked. Closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

places.name: Nepal Tourism Board permit desk
places.note: Where TIMS cards and ACAP permits are actually issued: two passport photos, cash in rupees, about NPR 3,000 for ACAP and NPR 2,000 for TIMS. Sunday to Friday, shut Saturdays, and the Pokhara office does the same job if you would rather not lose a Kathmandu morning.

places.name: The Thamel gear shops
places.note: Four blocks of North Face signage, perhaps one shop in ten selling genuine stock. Down jackets and sleeping bags rent for a few dollars a day and that is the right call; buy the trekking poles and the wool socks, and do not trust a 'Gore-Tex' shell at fifteen dollars.

places.name: Kopan Monastery
places.note: A Gelugpa monastery on a hill twenty minutes above Boudhanath, with 350 monks and a garden looking north to the Shivapuri ridge. Visitors can walk the grounds free in the morning; it is the quietest hour anywhere in the valley and almost nobody comes up.

places.name: Newa Lahana, Kirtipur
places.note: A community-run Newari kitchen on the Kirtipur ridge: bara, choila, sukuti, buffalo in nine forms, and aila poured from a jug, ordered off a laminated sheet with no English translation of half of it. Twenty minutes by taxi from Thamel and worth the fare.

places.name: Krishnarpan at Dwarika's
places.note: Six to twenty two courses of Nepali regional cooking in a hotel built out of salvaged Newar woodcarving. It is the most expensive meal in the country and the only one that treats gundruk and dhido as worth plating properly. Book two days out.

places.name: OR2K
places.note: Floor cushions, shoes off at the door, Middle Eastern vegetarian food and the one Thamel kitchen you can eat in the night before a flight without worrying. Full of trekkers, which is the point: this is where you find someone to share a jeep with.

places.name: Himalayan Java, Thamel
places.note: Nepali-grown arabica roasted in-country, properly, from a chain that started here in 1999. Relevant beyond the caffeine: it has reliable power and wifi, which matters when you are trying to confirm a Lukla flight the evening before.

places.name: Sam's Bar
places.note: An upstairs room papered floor to ceiling in expedition flags and scrawled notes, open since the 1980s. Cheap Gorkha beer, a guitar someone always picks up, and the place where guides, pilots and climbers actually drink rather than where they are marketed.

places.name: Nyatapola Temple, Taumadhi Square
places.note: Thirty metres and five roofs on a five-stage plinth, built 1702, and it has now stood through both the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes while newer things around it fell. Climb the plinth steps past the stone guardians; the doors are shut to visitors.

places.name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square and the 55-Window Palace
places.note: The NPR 1,800 ticket covers the whole walled town for as many days as you want, so get it stamped and come back at dawn. The Golden Gate and the 55 carved windows are the set piece; the Vatsala temple beside them is a 2021 reconstruction.

places.name: Pottery Square
places.note: Two dozen families still throwing unglazed blackware on kick wheels and drying it in the open square, which in monsoon means nothing is drying and nobody is working. Best October to May. You can sit at a wheel for a couple of dollars.

places.name: Dattatreya Square and the Peacock Window
places.note: The oldest square in town and the emptiest, five minutes east of the crowds. The Peacock Window is down a side lane off it, a 15th-century lattice that is the single best piece of Newar woodcarving in Nepal and is signposted almost not at all.

places.name: Juju dhau
places.note: King curd: buffalo milk yoghurt set in unglazed clay pots that wick out the water, so it comes out thick enough to hold a spoon upright. Sold from shopfronts around both squares for well under a dollar. Do not eat it on the morning you fly to Lukla.

places.name: The Nagarkot view tower at sunrise
places.note: A concrete tower at the end of the ridge with a claimed eight-range panorama. On a clear November dawn you get Langtang, Ganesh, Manaslu and a distant triangle of Everest; from March the haze usually eats all of it and nobody tells you that in advance.

places.name: The Nagarkot to Changu Narayan walk
places.note: Four hours mostly downhill along a farming ridge through terraces and pine, ending at Changu Narayan; you can send your bag ahead by taxi. The route is unmarked and braids constantly, so take a local guide or a GPS track rather than the hotel's hand-drawn map.

places.name: Changu Narayan temple
places.note: The oldest Hindu temple still in use in the valley, with a stone inscription dated 464 AD in the courtyard and a Garuda statue that appears on the rupee note. Badly damaged in 2015 and reopened; almost nobody comes, which is the reason to.

places.name: The Bandipur bazaar street
places.note: A Newar trading town from the old Kathmandu to India route, stranded when the Prithvi Highway went round it in the 1960s and therefore never rebuilt in concrete. The single street is closed to vehicles and is the best surviving 19th-century streetscape in Nepal.

places.name: Thani Mai and the Tundikhel
places.note: Thirty minutes of steps above the village to a small temple facing the whole Annapurna to Manaslu wall, and a second twenty minutes to the Tundikhel, a flat parade ground on a spur with a 1,000m drop off the far edge. Sunrise, then breakfast back down.

places.name: Siddha Gufa
places.note: One of the largest caves in Nepal: about 50m high inside, reached by 45 minutes of steep descent from Bandipur and a scramble at the mouth. Wet, unlit apart from a hired torch, and genuinely slippery. Skip it in monsoon.

places.name: The walk to Ramkot
places.note: Three hours return on a level ridge path to a Magar village of round thatched houses, with nobody selling you anything at the end of it. The best short walk in central Nepal and the reason to give Bandipur a full day rather than a night.

places.name: The Old Inn terrace
places.note: A restored Newar house at the top of the bazaar with a stone terrace hanging over the valley. The food is fine rather than remarkable; the reason to eat here is that the terrace faces Himalchuli and the light on it at 17:30 is the best hour of the drive day.

places.name: Phewa Lake and Tal Barahi
places.note: Row yourself out at 06:30 and the Annapurnas and Machhapuchhre are reflected in flat water for about forty minutes before the wind gets up and ruins it. Tal Barahi, the island temple, is five minutes off the shore and busy with pilgrims on Saturdays.

places.name: The World Peace Pagoda
places.note: A Japanese-built stupa at 1,113m on the ridge across the lake. Do it properly: boat to the far shore, 45 minutes up through forest, then walk the ridge on to Pumdikot. Taxis go to the door, which removes the only interesting part.

places.name: International Mountain Museum
places.note: Bigger and better than it looks from outside: the ethnography of the Sherpa, Thakali and Gurung, the full history of the 8,000m first ascents, and a genuinely sobering room on Himalayan glacier retreat. The obvious wet-afternoon two hours in Pokhara.

places.name: Devi's Fall and Gupteshwor Mahadev cave
places.note: The waterfall itself is a concreted sluice behind a railing and not worth the ticket. The cave across the road is: 3km of limestone passage, a Shiva lingam in a chamber at the bottom, and the fall coming through the roof at the far end. Go for the cave.

places.name: Begnas Lake
places.note: The lake Pokhara had before the paragliders: fish farms, a ridge walk up to Sundari Danda between Begnas and Rupa, and no lakeside strip. Twenty five minutes by taxi and effectively empty on a weekday. Fish thali at the jetty restaurants.

places.name: Old Bazaar and Bindhyabasini temple
places.note: Four kilometres northeast of Lakeside is the actual town: Newar shopfronts selling brass, cloth and seed, and a hilltop Kali temple where goats are sacrificed on Saturday mornings. Almost no tourist walks it, and it takes fifteen minutes by taxi to reach.

places.name: Gurkha Memorial Museum
places.note: Two floors on the Gurkha regiments, largely recruited from the hills you are about to walk into, with the citations for all thirteen Victoria Crosses. Small, unfashionable, and the piece of context most trekkers in Pokhara skip.

places.name: The Lakeside promenade
places.note: The paved shore path from the Barahi end south towards Damside, mostly quiet and unbuilt on the water side. Pleasant at dusk; touristy in daylight and the mountains are invisible from it after about 10:00 because the haze rises off the lake.

places.name: Pumdikot Shiva statue
places.note: A 108-foot Shiva finished in 2021 on the ridge south of the lake, floodlit at night and visible from most of Lakeside. Go for sunset and the walk along from the Peace Pagoda rather than for the statue, which is new concrete and looks it.

places.name: Moondance Restaurant
places.note: Open since the early 1990s and still the most reliable kitchen on the strip: steaks, wood-fired pizza, a real wine list and a fire in the room from November. Where people eat the night they come off the Annapurna trail and want something that is not dal bhat.

places.name: Caffe Concerto
places.note: An Italian-run wood-oven pizzeria with a lake-facing upstairs and opera on the stereo, which sounds unbearable and is not. Thin bases, proper mozzarella. Busy from 19:00 in season and there are only about ten tables upstairs.

places.name: Busy Bee Cafe
places.note: The one live-music bar in Pokhara that has lasted, with a covers band most nights from about 20:00 and a courtyard for when the room gets loud. Everything in Lakeside shuts by around 23:00 under a municipal rule, and this is where you are at 22:45.

places.name: Himalayan Java, Lakeside
places.note: Second-floor balcony over the main strip, decent flat white, and the practical stop for the morning you are sorting a jeep to the trailhead. Nepali beans from Gulmi and Kavre; ask for the single origin rather than the house blend.

places.name: Sarangkot at sunrise
places.note: Leave Lakeside at 05:00 and you get Dhaulagiri, the Annapurnas, Machhapuchhre and Manaslu going pink in one sweep, with Phewa Lake in cloud below. October to December is the reliable window; by April the pre-monsoon haze usually takes the western half.

places.name: Paragliding from Sarangkot
places.note: Tandem off the ridge and 1,000m down to Khapaudi on the lakeshore, 25 to 35 minutes, with vultures thermalling alongside. Flying is morning-only in stable air and stops entirely in monsoon. Check the operator's insurance; the safety record here is uneven.

places.name: The Sarangkot to Naudanda ridge walk
places.note: Four hours west along the ridgeline on the old Annapurna approach, with the range on your right the whole way and tea shops at Kaskikot and Naudanda. Flat, shadeless, and empty since the road to Baglung took the trekkers off it.

places.name: Ghandruk old village
places.note: Slate roofs, stone stairs and dry-stone walls at 1,940m, with Annapurna South and Hiunchuli filling the northern sky. The upper village above the school is where the old houses are; the lower is lodges and a car park. Everything here is stairs.

places.name: The Gurung Museum
places.note: Two rooms in a traditional house: the loom, the bamboo doko, the ceremonial dress, and a wall on Gurkha recruitment which is why so many of these houses were built. Twenty minutes, run by whoever is around, and the entry is a dollar in a box.

places.name: The Ghandruk viewpoint
places.note: Ten minutes above the top houses to an open shoulder facing Annapurna South at 7,219m, Hiunchuli and the Machhapuchhre fishtail. First light hits Annapurna South around 06:20 in November and the whole village is out watching it.

places.name: Ghandruk to Landruk across the Modi Khola
places.note: Down 600m of stone steps to the river at Syauli Bazaar, over the bridge and 500m back up the far side to Landruk. Five hours, brutal on the knees in both directions, and the classic short loop when you do not have days for the sanctuary.

places.name: The ACAP checkpost, Ghandruk
places.note: Where your ACAP permit and TIMS card are logged by hand in a ledger. Since April 2023 the rule is that trekkers here must have a licensed guide, and this is one of the posts that actually checks; turning up without either means being turned back.

places.name: The teahouse dal bhat in Ghandruk
places.note: Rice, lentil broth, a curried vegetable, greens and pickle, with refills of everything brought until you stop eating. It is the same meal at every lodge on every trek in Nepal for about seven dollars, and it is the only item cooked fresh in volume.

places.name: Poon Hill at sunrise
places.note: Forty five minutes and 340m up from Ghorepani in head-torch light to a tower facing Dhaulagiri at 8,167m and Annapurna South. In late October there can be two hundred people on it. Go anyway, and stay twenty minutes after the crowd leaves.

places.name: The Poon Hill tea stall
places.note: A shack at 3,210m selling instant coffee and boiled eggs to people who left their lodge at 04:45 in a fleece and are now shaking. Cash in rupees, no change for a 1,000, and it opens only through the trekking season.

places.name: The Ulleri staircase
places.note: Roughly 3,200 stone steps in one continuous flight up from Tikhedhunga to Ulleri, about 1,000m of gain with no flat anywhere in it. Three hours up, and it is the single hardest hour of the Poon Hill trek. Going down it is worse on the knees.

places.name: The rhododendron forest to Deurali and Tadapani
places.note: Six hours east from Ghorepani on a mossy ridge through old rhododendron, which flowers red and pink through late March and April and is simply a dark wood the rest of the year. Wet, rooty, and much better than retracing the way you came up.

places.name: The Ghorepani dining room stove
places.note: One iron stove in the middle of the room, lit around 17:00, and every wet sock in the building hung above it. The bedrooms are unheated plywood at 2,874m, so this is the only warm place; dinner orders are taken at 18:00 for everyone at once.

places.name: Birethanti and the Bhurungdi Khola
places.note: The trailhead village on a green river with a suspension bridge, a permit post and the last proper cafe. Two flat hours up the Bhurungdi to Tikhedhunga before the climbing starts, and the ACAP entry is checked here rather than further up.

places.name: Annapurna Base Camp, 4,130m
places.note: A grassy shelf inside a ring of 7,000m walls with Annapurna I directly above it, the only place in the Himalaya where you stand in a closed amphitheatre like this. Clear mornings go cloudy by 10:00 almost daily, so the view is at dawn or not at all.

places.name: Machhapuchhre Base Camp, 3,700m
places.note: Four lodges on a shoulder 430m below ABC, and the sensible place to sleep rather than pushing on and waking with a headache. Machhapuchhre itself has never been officially climbed; the 1957 attempt stopped 50m short by agreement and it has been closed since.

places.name: The Hinku Cave avalanche section
places.note: The 3km of narrow gorge between Deurali and MBC where the avalanche chutes come down, and where people have been killed, most recently in the 2014 and 2020 winters. Cross it early, before the sun loads the slopes, and not at all after heavy snow.

places.name: Bamboo, Dovan and Deurali
places.note: Three lodge clusters strung up a sunless bamboo and rhododendron gorge between 2,310m and 3,230m, on the one day of the trek with no view at all. Leeches after rain, landslide sections, and the lodges fill by 15:00 in October so start early.

places.name: Jhinu Danda hot springs
places.note: Three stone pools by the Modi Khola, twenty minutes steeply down from the lodges at Jhinu, fed at about 40C. It is the obvious thing to do on the way out with five days of walking in your legs. Busy from 16:00 and closed when the river runs high.

places.name: Mardi Himal High Camp, 3,580m
places.note: Six lodges on a bare ridge with Machhapuchhre 3km away and filling half the sky. There is no water source up here, so everything is carried up and prices reflect it, and the lodges are full by mid-afternoon in October with no alternative for two hours down.

places.name: Mardi Himal Viewpoint, 4,200m
places.note: Two to three hours up a narrowing ridge from High Camp, with a short exposed section on scree near the top that is genuinely unpleasant in snow or cloud. Turn round at Upper Viewpoint if the weather is in; the view from 4,200m is Annapurna I straight down the glacier.

places.name: Low Camp and the rhododendron ridge
places.note: Five hours of dripping moss forest and rhododendron tunnel along the ridge crest from Forest Camp, with the trees opening out at Badal Danda. The whole first half of this trek is inside cloud forest and the mountains only appear on day three.

places.name: Forest Camp, 2,520m
places.note: Where you sleep the first night out of Kande, after five hours of steep wet forest with leeches in it after rain. The trek only opened to teahouses in 2012, which is why the lodges are newer and the crowds smaller than on the Poon Hill side.

places.name: Dugout canoe on the Rapti
places.note: An hour drifting downstream in a hollowed sal trunk at eye level with mugger crocodiles and gharials on the bank, with kingfishers and storks the whole way. Do it at 06:30 in mist; the 15:00 trip is hot and the birds are gone.

places.name: Guided jungle walk in the core area
places.note: Four hours on foot with two licensed guides and no weapon between them, in a park with about 700 one-horned rhino and roughly 125 tigers. Rhino and sloth bear are the actual danger and people are injured most years. This is the real Chitwan experience.

places.name: Jeep safari to Kasara
places.note: A long, dusty, bone-shaking half day deep into the core area to the park headquarters, which is the only way to cover enough ground for a tiger sighting and still a long shot. Jeep access to the core area is periodically restricted, so confirm before booking.

places.name: Gharial Breeding Centre, Kasara
places.note: A hatchery running since 1978 that has released thousands of gharial into the Narayani and Rapti, because the wild population had collapsed to a few dozen. Tanks of animals by year class, and the only place you see a gharial's snout up close.

places.name: Elephant Breeding Centre, Khorsor
places.note: The government breeding stable, where the park's patrol elephants are raised. Worth an hour for the calves and the honest sight of chained adults; elephant-back safaris have been pushed out of the park itself and any operator still selling one is working the buffer zone.

places.name: Bis Hazari Tal
places.neighborhood: Twenty Thousand Lakes, north of the park
places.note: A Ramsar oxbow wetland in sal forest north of Sauraha with a boardwalk and a tower, and about 250 recorded bird species. Almost no lodge sells it, so you organise your own bicycle or jeep. Best December to February for the migratory waterfowl.

places.name: The Tharu village walk at Bachhauli
places.note: Mud-and-dung longhouses and the Tharu stick dance, performed nightly at the cultural centre in Sauraha. The dance show is a show; the walk through the village behind it at 16:00, with the livestock coming in, is the part worth your time.

places.name: The Rapti sunset point
places.note: A row of plastic chairs on the sand facing west across the river into the park, with cold Gorkha brought to you. Everyone in Sauraha is here at 17:30, elephants sometimes cross downstream, and it costs almost nothing.

places.name: Tenzing-Hillary Airport
places.note: A 527m runway on an 11.7 percent slope with a rock wall at one end and a drop at the other, flown visually. In peak season most flights are shifted to Manthali, four to five hours' drive east of Kathmandu, departing pre-dawn: confirm which airport you are leaving from.

places.name: The Pasang Lhamu memorial gate
places.note: The arch you walk under leaving town, named for the first Nepali woman to summit Everest, who died on the descent in 1993. It is where the trek actually starts and where the Khumbu municipality fee is checked on the way in.

places.name: Lukla to Phakding
places.note: Three easy hours mostly downhill to 2,610m, which is the right first day: you have just flown to 2,845m and dropping 200m to sleep is how acclimatisation is supposed to work. Do not let a guide push you on to Monjo on day one.

places.name: The Lukla lodge dal bhat
places.note: Everything above Lukla arrives on a porter's back or a mule, so prices climb about 15 percent per day of walking and dal bhat is the only meal with unlimited refills. Eat it here for nine dollars; at Gorak Shep the same plate is nearly twenty.

places.name: The Namche Saturday market
places.note: Traders come up from the lower valleys and, historically, over the Nangpa La from Tibet, and lay out vegetables, cloth and slaughtered meat on tarpaulins. Saturday mornings only, done by about 11:00, and the one day Namche is a Sherpa town rather than a trekking street.

places.name: Sagarmatha National Park visitor centre
places.note: A short climb above the village to a small museum on Sherpa settlement and park ecology, and a terrace with the first clear sight of Everest, Lhotse and Ama Dablam. The walk up is itself the standard acclimatisation errand on a Namche rest day.

places.name: Hotel Everest View, Syangboche
places.note: Two hours and 440m up to a Japanese-built hotel at 3,880m with a terrace facing Everest and Ama Dablam, where you drink a very expensive coffee and walk back down to sleep lower. Climb high, sleep low, made into an outing.

places.name: Khumjung and the monastery yeti scalp
places.note: The largest Sherpa village in the Khumbu, with Hillary's school, the Edmund Hillary memorial, and a monastery whose caretaker will unlock a case containing a conical 'yeti scalp' for a small donation. It was tested in 1960 and is goat.

places.name: Tengboche Monastery
places.note: The principal gompa of the Khumbu at 3,867m, burnt down in 1989 and rebuilt, framed dead-on by Ama Dablam. Visitors may sit at the back of the 15:00 puja. Mani Rimdu, the masked dance festival, falls in late October or November depending on the lunar calendar.

places.name: Namche to Tengboche via Phunki Tenga
places.note: Two easy hours contouring at 3,400m with Ama Dablam ahead the whole way, then 600m down to the river at Phunki Tenga and 600m straight back up through juniper to Tengboche. Six hours, and everyone underestimates the second half of it.

places.name: Sherpa Culture Museum
places.note: A private collection run by a local photographer: Sherpa household objects, a wall of every Nepali Everest summiteer, and honest labelling of how many died. Small and easy to miss, and better on the human cost of the mountain than the park centre.

places.name: Herman Helmer's Bakery
places.note: German-recipe apple strudel, cinnamon rolls and real coffee at 3,440m, baked on site. It is a cliche of the Khumbu and it is also where you will spend two hours on a rest day, because the alternative is sitting in an unheated room.

places.name: Cafe Danphe Bar
places.note: Pool table, Everest beer, a stove and guides off duty. Worth one night on the way up and none on the way down if you are still going higher: alcohol at 3,440m makes the next morning's climb measurably worse and every guide will tell you so.

places.name: Nangkartshang, 5,083m
places.note: The acclimatisation climb that decides whether the rest of the trek works: 670m up a bare ridge from 4,410m, three hours up and ninety minutes down, with Makalu appearing over the shoulder at the top. If this one hurts badly, going higher will hurt worse.

places.name: Dingboche's stone walls
places.note: Hundreds of dry-stone enclosures a metre high, built to keep yaks off barley and potatoes at 4,410m, which is close to the upper limit of cultivation anywhere. Walk the lanes in the late afternoon and you will understand the economics of the valley.

places.name: Pangboche monastery
places.note: The oldest gompa in the Khumbu, said to be founded in the 1660s, an hour below Dingboche and passed by nearly everyone without stopping. It held the famous yeti hand until it was stolen in the 1990s. The upper village is the old one; the lower is lodges.

places.name: Chhukhung and the Imja valley
places.note: Three hours up a flat glacial valley east of Dingboche under the south face of Lhotse, with Island Peak at the head of it. The better acclimatisation day than Nangkartshang if you have a spare one, and you will meet almost nobody on it.

places.name: Ama Dablam Base Camp, 4,600m
places.note: Two and a half hours across grazing land to a meadow under the southwest ridge of the most photographed mountain in Nepal. In October and November it is a working climbers' camp with tents and fixed lines going up; in spring it is empty grass.

places.name: The Dingboche lodge stove
places.note: A yak-dung stove lit at 17:00 in the only heated room in the building, and dung smoke at 4,410m is why half the valley develops the Khumbu cough. Ginger lemon honey by the pot, no alcohol above Namche, and lights out around 20:30.

places.name: Gorak Shep, 5,164m
places.note: Four lodges on the sand of a drained glacial lake beside the Khumbu Glacier, with about half the oxygen of sea level, no heating in the rooms and no real washing. Sleep one night. People who plan two usually come down after the first.

places.name: The Dughla Pass memorials
places.note: Around fifty stone chortens on the moraine crest at 4,830m for climbers and Sherpas who died on Everest, including Scott Fischer and the 2014 icefall dead. It is a 45-minute climb on the hardest section of the trail and nobody talks on the way up.

places.name: The Khumbu Glacier pinnacles
places.note: White seracs and ice pinnacles standing out of grey rubble directly above the lodges, and the closest you get to the mechanics of a Himalayan glacier without ropes. Walk out on the lateral moraine, not onto the ice, and go before the wind gets up.

places.name: The Gorak Shep dining room
places.note: Dal bhat for around eighteen dollars because everything here came 60km on a yak, hot water sold by the litre, and phone charging billed by the hour. Eat, drink three litres of water, and do not take a sleeping pill at 5,164m.

places.name: Kala Patthar, 5,545m
places.note: Three hundred and eighty metres up a black shoulder from Gorak Shep, two to three hours at a pace that feels absurd, for the only ground-level view of Everest's whole southwest face. Colder than anything else on the trek: minus 20C in the pre-dawn wind is normal.

places.name: Everest Base Camp, 5,364m
places.note: Four hours return from Gorak Shep over loose moraine to a painted rock and a lot of prayer flags. In April and May it is a tent city of several hundred climbers; in October it is bare ice and rubble. The view of Everest from it is blocked by Nuptse.

places.name: The Khumbu Icefall viewpoint
places.note: From base camp you look straight up into the icefall, 600m of collapsing blocks that every Everest summit has to cross, where sixteen Sherpas were killed in one 2014 serac collapse. Standing under it explains the whole economy of this mountain.

places.name: Syabrubesi and the Bhote Koshi bridge
places.note: A roadhead strip of lodges either side of a long suspension bridge over a grey glacial river, with a Chinese-built hydro scheme upstream. Nothing to do; the point is that the jeep stops here and the walking starts on the far bank.

places.name: Langtang National Park checkpost, Dhunche
places.note: Where the Langtang permit, about NPR 3,000, plus the TIMS card, is checked and stamped. Every vehicle stops and it takes twenty minutes. Since 2023 a licensed guide is formally required in the national parks, and this is a post that asks to see one.

places.name: The Trishuli road from Kathmandu
places.note: Seven to nine hours for 120km: tarmac to Trishuli, then single-lane gravel cut into a gorge wall with a 500m drop and no barrier, and landslide repairs most years. It is the worst day of the Langtang trek and it happens before you have walked a step.

places.name: The Syabrubesi lodge dal bhat
places.note: Six dollars, cooked over gas rather than a porter's back, and the cheapest plate of the whole trek because the road reaches here. The lodges are basic, the power goes off around 22:00, and you want to be walking by 07:30.

places.name: Kyanjin Gompa, 3,870m
places.note: A small monastery and a dozen rebuilt lodges at the head of the valley, under the ice of Langtang Lirung at 7,227m. This is the end of the trail for most people and the base for both acclimatisation hills; you need two nights, not one.

places.name: Tserko Ri, 4,984m
places.note: Eleven hundred metres of climbing from 3,870m, four hours up and two down, starting at 04:30 to be on top before the cloud. The reward is a 360 of Langtang Lirung, Langshisa Ri and the Tibetan border peaks. The single best day in the valley.

places.name: Kyanjin Ri, 4,300m
places.note: Ninety minutes straight up behind the lodges to a prayer-flag cairn at about 4,300m. This is the half-day version for the afternoon you arrive, and doing it makes Tserko Ri the next morning far more likely to go well.

places.name: Langtang village and the avalanche memorial
places.note: On 25 April 2015 the earthquake released an ice avalanche off Langtang Lirung that erased the village and killed around 250 people, including most of one extended family. It has been rebuilt slightly uphill. The memorial boulder and the debris field are both still there.

places.name: The Kyanjin yak cheese factory
places.note: A Swiss-assisted dairy from the 1950s still pressing hard cheese from nak milk at 3,870m, sold by the slab. Buy 200g for the walk out; it is the one local product in Nepal that would survive being taken home.

places.name: The Langtang Lirung glacier moraine
places.note: A flat two hours up the valley floor onto the lateral moraine below the Lirung icefall, with rockfall coming off it at intervals you can hear. Easy and almost nobody does it, because everyone is resting for Tserko Ri.
